extracted.intended_audience: Parliamentarians, government officials, administrative agency policymakers, and legal/advisory bodies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and recommended statutory process standards for independent administrative agencies, addressing accountability, rulemaking, notice, participation, delegation, executive oversight, and related procedural safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accountability rendered directly to Parliament
rubrics_metrics.description: The accountability that agencies owe to Parliament should, in the normal course, be rendered directly to Parliament through its committee structure, not through the executive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whatever supervision Cabinet exercises is delegated; the duty to account is still owed to Parliament. Parliament should be careful about delegating supervisory responsibility to the executive for fear it may seriously compromise goals of independent decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent/enabling Acts define broad objectives clearly
rubrics_metrics.description: The constituent and enabling Acts relating to an independent administrative agency should define its broad objectives as clearly and in as plain and as unambiguous language as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These Acts should not normally attempt to spell out detailed policies required to implement objectives. The dynamic nature of administration frequently requires further structuring of policy within subordinate legislation and within the agency's own rule-making and decision-making processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary assent required to redefine agency role
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary assent is essential where the goal is not merely to clarify how the agency pursues legislative objectives, but to redefine its role and duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequently, parliamentary approval should be required through an affirmative resolution procedure whenever the authority provided for by the Public Service Rearrangement and Transfer of Duties Act is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency dominance in subordinate legislative process
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of the relationship between statutory decision making and policy development, and the importance of broad participation, independent administrative agencies should play a dominant role in whatever subordinate legislative process is provided for by statute.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agencies should be central actors in shaping subordinate legislation that prescribes policy guiding agency decision making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal regulation-making authority to agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: It is frequently desirable that regulation-making authority be given formally to an agency. Where the mandate of an agency necessarily involves it in matters of policy, it should, in principle, be authorized to develop policy in the form of regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These regulations should not normally be subject to executive approval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pilot: exempt agency regs submitted to notice/comments from prereg requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: A pilot project should be undertaken exempting agency regulations that are submitted to a public notice and comment procedure from those requirements of the Statutory Instruments Act that precede registration and publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is to streamline rulemaking where public notice and comment provides the substantive transparency intended by registration/publication requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy directions authority limited and legislative in form
rubrics_metrics.description: Authority to issue policy directions to independent administrative agencies should only exist where the agency has a broad mandate to develop and apply policies in areas of activity that Parliament determines, on a statute-by-statute basis, to be suitable for executive guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It should not be possible to issue directions to agencies that perform solely adjudicative or courtlike functions. Where authorized, directions should be issued by Cabinet, not by an individual minister, and should take the form of regulations — legislative, not decisional in nature and effect — addressing general policy issues in advance of specific cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory authority for non-binding policy statements and crystallization
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be given the statutory authority to formulate non-binding policy statements about how they will exercise their discretion or interpret their legislation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authority should be given to permit non-binding policy statements to crystallize into binding ones whenever the agency develops a firm view of the policy that ought to condition its exercise of discretion in individual cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary committee oversight of subordinate legislation and policy
rubrics_metrics.description: All subordinate legislation prescribing policy for statutory decision making by independent administrative agencies, and all binding policy statements adopted by an agency, should fall within the purview of the Standing Joint Committee on Regulations and Other Statutory Instruments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This places subordinate legislative policy and binding agency policy statements under parliamentary scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary disallowance procedure for regulations/policy statements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Statutory Instruments Act should be amended to allow for a general procedure by which Parliament could disallow regulations or policy statements adopted by the executive or an agency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides Parliament a formal mechanism to check subordinate legislation or agency policy instruments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active parliamentary monitoring and committee mandates
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should take steps to ensure that administrative policy evolves in an orderly and open fashion; Parliament and parliamentary committees should be more active in monitoring and reviewing the exercise of subordinate legislative authority relating to agency activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Committees should have a clear mandate to scrutinize the activities of particular agencies, and should exert influence over the shape and content of agency reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use parliamentary mechanisms efficiently (including sunsets)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although a strengthened committee system would make the use of new techniques such as 'sunset' provisions more feasible, Parliament should use more efficiently existing mechanisms of parliamentary democracy to hold agencies accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourages better use of tools already available before introducing new mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: No executive appeal/review at instance of interested party
rubrics_metrics.description: Decisions by independent administrative agencies should not be open to executive appeal or review at the instance of an interested party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeal or review should be to other agencies or to courts, not to political authorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visibility and political accountability for intrusive executive authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrusive executive authority affecting administrative decision making should be both visible and politically accountable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a political check on an agency's decisions is imposed by statute, the Cabinet, but not a minister, should be authorized to vary or rescind the decision or to remove the power of decision from the agency. The availability and exercise of this power should be exceptional, but available at any point in the process. When exercised, it should be clear the issue is taken into the political arena and interested persons should be given an opportunity to make representations before the decision is made.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedures when high incidence of political control is contemplated
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a high incidence of political control is contemplated, it may be preferable to subject agency decisions to routine executive approval.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In these cases Cabinet should be required to: refer a matter back to the agency before refusing approval because of a concern not addressed; communicate an explanation of its refusal; and give policy directions from time to time to assist the agency. Even when subject to systematic approval, agency independence should be respected to maintain integrity of the agency process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Privative clauses should be abolished or plainly expressed
rubrics_metrics.description: Privative clauses, as presently composed, should be abolished. If a special provision is felt necessary to insulate agency decisions from judicial review, it should be expressed in plain language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a clause should direct courts to show deference to agency expertise and not exercise discretion to intervene unless the agency's interpretation of a legislative provision it administers is patently unreasonable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage agencies to intervene in judicial review to support jurisdiction
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should be encouraged to intervene to support their jurisdiction when it is challenged in judicial review proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proactive agency involvement in litigation can help protect or clarify jurisdictional boundaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliament should legislate basic process standards for agencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament should enunciate in legislation basic process standards that would apply to all independent administrative agencies; these standards are the foundation upon which agency rules would be based.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standards would not be rules of procedure themselves but foundations. Particularized procedures must reflect each agency's mandate; agencies must play a dominant role in transforming process standards into rules. Legislating standards has educational impact on agencies and the public, consolidates fundamental principles, helps adapt Charter requirements to administrative needs, and prevents over-reliance on judicial enforcement of general constitutional concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensuring reasonable and adequate notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies should ensure that all interested persons are given reasonable and adequate notice of agency proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ‘Reasonable and adequate notice’ includes timely notice that a proceeding will take place, information about the nature of the proceeding, the time and place of any hearing or appropriate time for written comment, and a fair indication of the issues to be raised. An 'interested person' may be someone who invoked jurisdiction, a participant in ongoing proceedings, or someone not yet involved but likely affected or able to contribute. Agencies have a duty to ensure notice is given and may impose the obligation on the person invoking jurisdiction. What constitutes reasonable notice varies with the proceeding; a person aggrieved by a determination affecting rights should get personalized notice, while rulemaking may use general public announcements, except where identifiable affected persons merit personalized notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowing communication of information and views (participant rights)
rubrics_metrics.description: Those entitled to receive notice must be accorded standing as participants and should have a reasonable opportunity to communicate information and views to the agency, and to comment on submissions of other participants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Information that may influence the agency should be subject to critical examination by all participants, consistent with confidentiality. This does not require formal hearings or oral presentations in all cases; modes of participation should be chosen according to the issues. Participants need not have equal opportunities; consolidation of interventions may be warranted. The standard emphasizes function over method to encourage innovative means of obtaining information. Agencies may delegate data-collection or hearing functions — e.g., panels, single members, staff, or external hearing officers presiding over hearings — depending on needs and constraints.
